use of opiates in the State of Maine.
Hamilton Wright, who visited us for
a few days several weeks ago, is
quoted as saying that he discovered,
or was told, that there were Maine
people who used drugs because they
could not get liquor. The statements
attributed to Mr. Wright made, if ap
pear, by inference at least, that the
use of opiates was increasing in
Maine. The physicians and druggists
with whom DIR. Young communicated
say on the other hand that instead of
increasing, the use of such drugs in
Maine is on the decrease. Only ore
man takes a view of the situation
similar to that which is said to have
been given publicity by Mr.. Wright.
DR.. Young has long been the secre-
tary of the board OF health. He is a
man whose work has been done in a
manner to earn the confidence of the
people of the state and his conclu-
sions are entitled to respect. He
finds that as matter OF fact there is
reason for congratulations that Maine
people are less addicted to the use of
Injurious drugs than they have been
in the past and that there is no cause
for alarm in connection with the
question.


1t is significant that in many of the
replies received by DIR. Young to his
inquiries, it is stated that the de-
crease in the use of opiates is due to
greater care by physicians in pre-
scribing such drugs. 1t is obvious
that the habit of using opiates is
much more likely to be acquired by
persons made familiar with their eff
fects when taken first by advice OF
doctor than from any other cause.

erately begin the use of a drug con
corning which he has only hearsay
knowledge. This tact is recognized
by physicians themselves and there
is a constantly increasing caution on
their part in prescribing opiates.
This caution is rendered possible in
many cases by an increased knowl-
edge of remedies which may be used
without danger. Thus it appears
that in the judgment of druggists and
physicians there WIS time when
more people in the state were given
to the use of opiates than at present;
that this was due to the more general
use of such drugs in the first place as
the result Ct advice by doctors and
that the decrease which is reported
is due in large measure to the change
in the practice of physicians in deal
ing with situation calling for the
exercise of great care and judgment.
The prohibitory law has little if any
thing to do with the matter.

shall enable homesteaders of right to occupy and
acquire title to all portions thereof which are es-
pecially adapted to agriculture and which shall fur-
nish system of timber sales available as well to the
private citizen as to the larger manufactures and
consumer


Local government is demanded for Alaska and
Porto Rico, along with declaration of the intention
of the nation to recognize the independence of the
Philippine islands "as as stable government
can be established, such independence be guaran-
teed until naturalization of the islands can be se-
cured by treaties with the other powers." The
Panama canal project meets with the expressed ap-
proval of the democratic party and an adequate navy
is favored. protest is made against Asiatic immi-
gration. Free grazing on public land outside of res-
ervations is advocated.


On the subject of trusts the platform says:


Private monopoly is indefensible and intolerable.
We therefore, favor the vigorous enforcement of the
criminal law against guilty trust magnates and off-
icals and demand the enactment of such additional
legislation as may be necessary to make it impossible
for private monopoly to exist in the United States.


Among the additional remedies we specify first
a law preventing duplication of directors among
corporations, second, a license system which will
without abridging the right of each state to create
corporations, or its right to regulate it, will for

watered stock and to prohibit the control by such

corporations to sell to all purchasers in all parts
of the country on the same terms after making due
allowance for cost of transportation.

favoritism. We invite the cooperation of all re-
